criterion_notes.c1: Examines water supply, sewerage, and sanitation only as part of bundled municipal urban infrastructure alongside roads, bridges, tunnels, subways, gas, heating, and parks; mentions urban tap water coverage, state working unit utility provision, and municipal wastewater treatment.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 because it examines institutional, fiscal, and administrative governance factors in China (central-local fiscal decentralisation, local tax assignment, extra-budgetary municipal capital financing via land leases/bonds/loans/connection fees, and municipal urban construction bureau autonomy). Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because it focuses on macro-level intergovernmental fiscal relations and general municipal capital construction financing/administration across bundled urban infrastructure rather than analysing a rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative policy and institutional overview synthesizing secondary literature, World Bank reports, and descriptive summary tables from published official statistical yearbooks, with an illustrative narrative profile of Shanghai; contains no primary data, no identifiable empirical methodology (quantitative, qualitative, or socio-legal), and is not a systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Table 2 and Table 5 reproduce descriptive secondary statistical yearbook indicators including urban tap water access percentage (already 100.0% in Shanghai in both 1990 and 1996) and per capita annual domestic water consumption, alongside road space, gas access, public transit, and municipal wastewater treatment percentage.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design and does not establish an analytical unit of analysis, exposure, and household/community water or sanitation access outcome relationship beyond macro-level narrative description and secondary statistical tables.

evidence_quotes.quote: Most urban residents have access to tap water, gas and public transport (see Table 2). Water supply coverage has already reached close to 95 per cent in urban China.
Related to urban construction, an urban land-use tax, a real estate tax and an urban maintenance and construction tax are now among the local taxes.
the Public Utility Bureau often has several subordinate entities that are in charge of water supply and drainage, residential gas and heating supply, and public transport.
First, municipal authorities have increased user charges for some infrastructure services including bus fares, gas supplies, water, wastewater discharge

Improvements are particularly rapid in road construction, park expansion and wastewater treatment. Compared to an average level of about 7 per cent in all Chinese cities, Shanghai now treats 30 per cent of its wastewater.

raw_response.exposure: Central-local fiscal decentralisation, municipal infrastructure capital financing mechanisms (earmarked taxes, extra-budgetary funds, land leases, bonds, loans, connection fees), and municipal urban construction organisational autonomy
raw_response.outcome: Descriptive secondary municipal infrastructure revenue/investment totals and aggregate urban indicators (paved road area, public transit, gas access, open space, tap water coverage percentage, per capita domestic water consumption, and municipal wastewater treatment percentage/capacity)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Chinese cities in aggregate secondary statistics (658 cities, 1990-1996) and Shanghai municipality (illustrative municipal profile, 1990-1996); no primary empirical sample
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence). Wu (1999) is a macro-level policy and institutional overview of urban infrastructure financing and municipal construction administration in post-1979 China, supplemented by an illustrative narrative profile of Shanghai based on secondary literature and published statistical yearbook aggregates (Tables 2, 3, 5, and 6). It has no primary data collection, no identifiable quantitative, qualitative, or socio-legal empirical methodology, and is not a systematic synthesis. In addition, while it satisfies the plain wording of Criterion 2 as an institutional/fiscal governance overview, it fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading because it examines intergovernmental fiscal revenue-sharing, capital financing instruments (taxes, land leases, bonds, loans), and municipal capital-budgeting bureaucracy across bundled infrastructure sectors (roads, bridges, subways, gas, water, sewerage) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Because it lacks an empirical method and identifiable study design, plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.
raw_response.study_design: Narrative policy and institutional overview (non-empirical; uses descriptive secondary statistical tables)
